rfHint: used for the Sharpe ratio and the capital market line
adjusted: These correlations cannot all hold at once (the matrix is not positive definite). To compute, I shrank all of them by {{pct}} towards zero; the values used are in the table.
chartAria: {{n}} random portfolios of {{assets}} assets and the efficient frontier. Minimum variance: return {{mvRet}}, vol {{mvVol}}. Maximum Sharpe: return {{msRet}}, vol {{msVol}}, Sharpe {{sharpe}}.
obs: The minimum-variance portfolio has a vol of {{mvVol}}, below the least volatile asset ({{minAssetVol}}): that is the diversification benefit when correlations are below 1. The maximum-Sharpe portfolio ({{sharpe}}) is where the line from r_f = {{rf}} touches the frontier. Raise the correlations to watch the curve straighten and that benefit disappear.
obsNoDiv: The minimum-variance portfolio has a vol of {{mvVol}}, practically that of the least volatile asset ({{minAssetVol}}): with these correlations there is almost no diversification benefit. The maximum-Sharpe portfolio ({{sharpe}}) is where the line from r_f = {{rf}} touches the frontier. Lower the correlations to make the curve bend left again.
note: Synthetic assets and parameters, long-only (no short selling) and parameters assumed known. In practice, expected returns estimated with error change the weights a lot. Educational content, not investment advice.
formulaText: w are the weights (w ≥ 0, summing to 1), μ the expected returns and Σ the covariance matrix, Σ<sub>ij</sub> = ρ<sub>ij</sub>σ<sub>i</sub>σ<sub>j</sub>. With up to 4 assets the code scans every portfolio on a 1% grid and keeps, for each return level, the one with the lowest vol: that is the frontier. Max Sharpe is the portfolio with the highest (μ<sub>p</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>)/σ<sub>p</sub>. If the correlation matrix is not positive definite (Cholesky test), it is shrunk towards the identity.
